p.seg: Preface
*Hàn Shū · Yìwén Zhì* (漢書·藝文志, Book of Han, Treatise on Literature) on the Miscellaneous School:
"The *Shī Zǐ* (尸子) in twenty chapters."
The *Suí Táng Zhì* (隋唐志, Catalogues of the Sui and Tang Dynasties) also states the same.
By the Sòng (宋) dynasty, the entire book had already been lost.
Wáng Yīnglín's (王應麟) *Hàn Zhì Kǎozhèng* (漢志考證, Textual Research on the Treatise on Literature of the Han) states:
"The *Lǐ Shū Shūmù* (李淑書目, Catalogue of Books by Lǐ Shū) preserved four *juàn* (卷, scrolls/chapters),
while the *Guǎngé Shūmù* (館閣書目, Catalogue of Books in the Imperial Library) only preserved two *piān* (篇, sections/articles),
combined into one *juàn*."
None of these versions were transmitted.
The ones transmitted in recent times
include the Rèn (任) family version from Zhènzé (震澤), the Huì (惠) family version from Yuánhé (元和), and the Sūn (孫) family version from Yánghú (陽湖).
The Rèn version consists of three *piān*:
"Rén Yì" (仁意, Benevolence and Righteousness),
"Jūn Zhì" (君治, Governance of the Ruler),
and "Guǎng Shì" (廣釋, Extensive Explanation).
In reality, they are all gleanings of lost writings,
forcibly matched to the old headings.
Jì Péi (繼培) initially read this book
and, based on what he had gathered,
marked the sources,
corrected the omissions and errors,
and rectified the text.
Later, he obtained the book from the Huì family
to compare and collate it,
and again found some doubts and discrepancies.
Therefore, he collected his usual commentaries,
I have made slight revisions.
The content recorded in the *Qúnshū Zhìyào* is taken as the upper volume,
and quotations from various books that are identical to it are annotated below.
What is not found in the *Zhìyào* but scattered in various books is taken as the lower volume.
Incorrect quotations and errors in various editions are listed separately as "Doubts,"
appended at the end.
I have carefully examined the *Liú Xiàng Biélù*,
which states that the book *Shī Zǐ* contains more than 60,000 words in total.
The present compilation
probably recovers only two out of ten parts,
which is regrettable.
However, from what can be generally seen, one can infer the complete details,
and there are still things that can be understood.
Zhāng Zhàn, in his commentary on the *Lièzǐ*,
states in his preface:
"The *Zhuāngzǐ*, *Shèn Dào*, *Hán Fēi*, *Shī Zǐ*, and *Huáinán*
all reveal the ultimate meaning of profoundness
and often quote their words."
Now, according to the "returning person" (歸人) saying, which appears in the "Tiānrùi Piān" (天瑞篇),
and the "words and actions echo shadows" (言行響影) saying, which appears in the "Shuōfú Piān" (說符篇),
what he recited and narrated was definitely not just a few words.
The *Huáinánzǐ · Zhuì Xíng Xùn* (淮南子·墜形訓) states:
"Pearls are found in water that is round and refracting,
jade is found in water that is square and refracting,
gold is found in clear water,
and jade flowers are found in Dragon Abyss."
It also states:
"The North Pole has ice that never melts."
Their sayings all originate from the *Shi Zi*.
Crown Prince Zhanghuai, annotating the *Book of the Later Han*,
stated that the *Shi Zi* consists of "twenty chapters,
nineteen of which discuss the principles of morality, benevolence, and righteousness,
and one of which discusses the perilous terrain of the nine provinces,
and the sources of water."
The text of the "Zhui Xing" (Fallen Forms) chapter should be in this chapter.
Based on this standard,

it can be known that the discussions in the "Zhui Xing Xun" (Instruction on Fallen Forms) regarding the "nine mountains," "nine passes," "nine marshes," and "water sources" must all derive from the *Shi Zi*.
Furthermore, by citing "redeeming people" we know it refers to the matter of Zǐ Gòng;
by citing "pleasing those near and attracting those from afar" we know it refers to Yè Gōng inquiring about governance;
by citing "Tāng's virtue extending to birds and beasts" we know it refers to releasing nets.
Extending from similar instances,
demanding substance from emptiness,
this lies in the profound contemplation of diligent scholars.
Liú Xiàng, in his preface to the *Xún Zǐ*, stated that the *Shi Zi's* writings "do not follow the laws of the former kings,
nor do they adhere to the techniques of Kǒng Shì."
Liú Xié also stated that it "comprehensively integrates various techniques,
with the techniques being thorough but the writing dull."
Now that the original book is lost,
its grand meaning cannot be fully grasped.
Various scholars, citing its sayings,
generally aim to select its essence,
pruning away its branches and leaves,
single words and remaining meanings,
which are all the more worthy of cherishing.
Its original book,
was at times secretly appropriated by people of old,
Later scholars often drew and borrowed from them,
passing on and imitating each other.
Now, I will briefly extract from each book,
roughly clarifying their origins,
in order to demonstrate and explain their similarities and differences.
The *Shǐjì* "Biography of Mèngzǐ and Xúnzǐ" mentions that the state of Chǔ had a Shīzǐ.
The *Jíjiě* commentary cites Liú Xiàng's *Biélù*, saying:
"The state of Chǔ had a Shīzǐ,
suspected to be located in Shǔ.
Now, according to the book *Shīzǐ*,
he was a person from Jìn,
named Jiǎo,
a retainer of the Qín minister Wèi Yāng.
Wèi Yāng, the Lord Shāng, in his scheming and planning,
establishing laws and governing the people,
never failed to consult with Jiǎo.
When Lord Shāng was executed,
Jiǎo feared being implicated and punished,
so he fled and escaped into Shǔ."
In the *Hànzhì*, Bān Gù's own commentary also identifies Jiǎo as a person from Lǔ.
The characters Jìn and Lǔ are similar in shape,
so it is not possible to definitively determine whether this is the case.

Learning without weariness
is the way to govern oneself;
teaching without impatience
is the way to govern others.
Now, silkworm cocoons,
if left unattended and unmanaged,
will rot and be discarded.
But if female workers reel the silk from them,
to make beautiful brocade,
the great ruler wears it to court.
The body is like a silkworm cocoon;
if left unattended and unmanaged, knowledge and conduct will decay.
But if wise men teach it,
to make it a worthy scholar,
then all the feudal lords in the world will dare not but respect him.
Therefore, Zǐ Lù,
was a rustic from Biàn;
Zǐ Gòng,
was a merchant from Wèi;
Yán Zhuōjù,
was a thief;
Zhuānsūn Shī,
was a horse trader.
Kǒngzǐ taught them,
and all became prominent scholars.
Now, learning is like sharpening.
Suppose you have Kūnwú metal and Zhūfù tin,
and have the artisans of Gànyuè,
cast them into a sword, but do not add grinding and sharpening,
then stabbing with it will not penetrate,
and striking with it will not cut.
But if you grind it with a whetstone,
加之以黃砥，
則其刺也無前，
其擊也無下。 Add to it a yellow whetstone, then its thrust will be without compare in front, its strike will be without compare below.
自是觀之，
礪之與弗礪其相去遠矣。 From this perspective, the difference between sharpening and not sharpening is vast.
今人皆知礪其劍，
而弗知礪其身。 People nowadays all know how to sharpen their swords, but do not know how to sharpen themselves.
夫學，
身之礪砥也。 Indeed, learning is the whetstone for the self.
夫子曰：
「車唯恐地之不堅也，
舟唯恐水之不深也。」 Confucius said: "The cart fears only that the ground is not firm enough, the boat fears only that the water is not deep enough."
有其器則以人之難為易，
夫道以人之難為易也。 Having the right tools transforms what is difficult for people into what is easy. Indeed, the Dao transforms what is difficult for people into what is easy.
是故 Zēngzǐ 曰：
「父母愛之，
喜而不忘；
父母惡之，
懼而無咎。」 Therefore, Zēngzǐ said: "If parents love you, be happy and do not forget [their kindness]; if parents dislike you, be fearful and do not incur blame."
然則愛與惡，
其於成孝無擇也。 Thus, love and dislike are both acceptable for achieving filial piety.
史鰌曰：
親而近之，
至敬以遜；
貌而疏之，
敬無怨。」 Shǐ Qiū said: "To the ruler, if he is close to you, approach him with utmost respect and deference; if he appears distant, maintain respect without resentment."
然則親與疏，
In achieving loyalty, there is nothing that should be rejected.

"[He] finds pleasure in the constraint of the ǐn kuò,
rectifies himself but does not rectify others,
and when goodness is abandoned, he is not resentful.
This is the conduct of Qū Bóyù."
Therefore, success and failure,
in achieving goodness, there is nothing that should be rejected.
Qū Hóu Fù said:

Observe what they distribute when wealthy,
what they promote when influential,

Therefore, poverty and success,
in achieving worthiness, there is nothing that should be rejected.
Therefore, love and hate, intimacy and distance, abandonment and promotion, poverty and success, all can be used to achieve righteousness,

Duke Huán's selection of Guǎn Zhòng,
Duke Mù's selection of Bǎilǐ,
were based on comparing their virtue.
This is why their states, though very remote and small,
and their persons, though very lowly and defiled,
could govern the world.
Now, if we do not compare their aspirations but compare their appearances,
if we do not compare their moral conduct but discuss their ranks and titles,
how can we repel enemies and subdue those far away?
Farmers are compared by their grain,
merchants are compared by their wealth,

Therefore, even gatekeepers, innkeepers, farmers, and potters can participate in it.
Official ranks
are private forms of nobility;
virtuous conduct
is public nobility.
How do we know this is so?

His servant said:
"He is merely a person from Chéngfēng;
why do you dismount for him?"
Zǐhǎn said:

Now, here is a person with heavenly nobility,

Viewing it from this perspective,
what was called nobility in ancient times was not official rank,

A ruler is noble within a country but does not extend his influence to the whole world;

Only virtuous conduct endures alongside heaven and earth.
Official ranks

the places where it resides.

Luxuriant is the sweet pear-tree,

The place where the benevolent man rests,

The Son of Heaven and the feudal lords,

Now, the accumulation of learning

There has never been a case of someone understanding the Dao without relying on learning,
nor of someone glorifying themselves without resorting to learning.

The ruler said,

None of the officials answered.
A boatman, Qīng Juān, put down his oar and answered,

The ruler said,

The ruler said,
"Excellent words!"
The next morning,
he ordered that the boatman Qīng Juān be rewarded with ten thousand *mǔ* of land.
He ordered that ten thousand *mǔ* of clear, clean fields be bestowed upon the boatman.
Qīng Juān declined.
The ruler said:
"With these fields,
in exchange for his words,
even if you were to lose them,
I would still gain."
The ancients valued words in this way.
To make subjects of the world,
is to unify the world.
To unify the world
is to make commands that are followed throughout the world,
and prohibitions that are obeyed.
Jié and Zhòu commanded the world, but were not followed;
they prohibited, but were not obeyed,
therefore, they did not gain subjects.
What the eyes find beautiful,
but the heart deems unrighteous,
one dares not look upon.
What the mouth finds delicious,
but the heart deems unrighteous,
one dares not eat.
What the ears find pleasing,
but the heart deems unrighteous,

What the body finds comfortable,
but the heart deems unrighteous,
one dares not wear.
Therefore, to make commands that are followed throughout the world, and prohibitions that are obeyed,
depends on the heart.
Therefore, it is said:
"The heart
is the ruler of the body."
The Son of Heaven receives commands from the heart in governing the world.
Easy to stop;
but by the time they burned Yúnmèng and Mèngzhū,
even if using the labor of the whole country
to drain the waters of the Yangtze and Han rivers,
it would be impossible to save them.
The beginning of a disaster
is like a spark that scorches the foot,
easy to stop.
But when it is applied to great affairs,
even with the wisdom of Kǒngzǐ and Mòdí,
it would be impossible to save them.
If a house burns down and people save it,
then they are grateful for the virtue;
if old people are made to plaster cracks and guard against leaks,
they will have no fire troubles for their whole lives,
yet they do not know the virtue.
Those who are imprisoned and released from hardship,
their entire family are grateful for the virtue;
if they are taught benevolence, righteousness, kindness, and brotherly love, they will have no troubles for their whole lives,
yet no one is grateful for the virtue.
Disasters also have leaks;
when the wise travel the world and strive to block them,
then the world will have no war troubles,
yet no one knows the virtue.
Therefore, it is said: "Sages govern with the spiritual,
fools contend with the obvious."
The Way of Heaven and Earth,
no one sees how it nurtures things, yet things grow;
Do not see the reason why things are lost, and yet things are lost.
The Dao of the sage is also like this.
When he brings about fortune,
people do not see it, yet fortune arises.
When he removes calamity,
people do not know it, yet calamity is removed.
Therefore, he is called "divine man" (shén rén).
To benefit the world with wealth is called "benevolence" (rén).
To exert the world with strength is called "righteousness" (yì).
To apportion the world so that all may live is called "divinity" (shén).
To cultivate the methods of the former kings,
to remove the root of disaster and difficulty,
to enable all the men in the world to plow and eat,
and the women to weave and clothe themselves,
so that all can keep their heads (i.e., live),
and fathers and sons can protect each other,
this is apportioning the myriad things so that all may live,
and benefiting the world with wealth,
beyond calculation.
Divinity (shén),
is the beginning of the myriad things,
the guideline for the myriad things.
Four Standards (sì yí)
Acting has four standards:
First, in the movement of intention, do not forget benevolence (rén).
Second, in the application of wisdom, do not forget righteousness (yì).
Third, in the use of strength, do not forget loyalty (zhōng).
Fourth, in the words of the mouth, do not forget trustworthiness (xìn).
Carefully guarding the four standards,
to the end of one's life,
fame and achievement will follow it,
just as a form has a shadow,
and a sound has an echo.
Therefore, if the mind does not forget benevolence,
then the center will be able to be generous and magnanimous;
if wisdom does not forget righteousness,
then conduct will have elegance and principle;
if strength does not forget loyalty,
then action will not be without accomplished merit;
if the mouth does not forget trustworthiness,
then words will be like tally sticks.
If the center is generous and magnanimous and conduct has elegance and principle,
actions have merit and words are trustworthy,
then even those of antiquity who had great accomplishments and great fame,
seen beyond the four seas,
known after ten thousand generations,
their personal conduct
was no more than this.
*Míng Táng*,
that is, high rank, prominence, and noble status,
is a shortcut to benefiting the world,
but it is not something that the benevolent lightly value.
How do we know that this is the case?
The sun's ability to shine far
is due to its high position;
if the sun were in a well,
Then it cannot illuminate ten steps.
When Shùn 舜 was making pottery,
he could not benefit those in his lane;
when he faced south and ruled the world,
the Mányí 蠻夷, Róngdí 戎狄 all received his blessings.
If the eye is at one's feet,
then it cannot see.
Heaven is high and bright,
therefore it can illuminate all things;
the earth is wide and vast,
therefore it can carry and support all creatures.
If its root is not beautiful,
then its branches, leaves, stems, and heartwood cannot be beautiful.
This is the great path of ancient and modern times,
therefore the sage kings carefully cultivate themselves in order to rule the world,
then the way of Heaven arrives,
the way of Earth conforms,
and all things are measured.
In ancient times, when enlightened kings sought out the worthy,
they did not avoid those who were far or near,
nor did they discuss those who were noble or base,
they lowered their ranks to employ the worthy,
and regarded their own persons as of little importance in order to put scholars first.
Therefore, Yáo 堯 followed Shùn 舜 from among the fields,
faced north to meet him,
and did not dispute matters of etiquette.
This is the reason why the former kings were able to rectify Heaven and Earth and benefit all things.

Now, the speaker harbors apprehension while the listener harbors arrogance,
to practice righteousness in this way,

That one has not sought out the worthy, employed scholars, and yet been able to achieve great renown throughout the world,
I have never heard of such a thing.
Scholars cannot be rashly acquired.

then qílín will not go there;
if you drain the pond to catch the fish,

Even foolish birds and beasts cannot be rashly acquired,

Therefore, it is said:

when listening to words,
one's ears and eyes are not attentive,

They are great because they are lower!"

people are great because they are lower than all the scholars in the world.

Therefore, looking back at the past,
observing the former kings,

There has never been such a case.

I have never seen such a case.

Regulate things by controlling their allocation,
